lectures.title: The Culinary Professional and the Chef as Manager
The Development of the Professional Kitchen and the Changing Role of the Chef
Kitchen Organisation I: The Partie System and the Brigade
Kitchen Organisation II: Staff, Roles and Responsibilities

cards.f: Define management (Ninemeier, 2000).
cards.b: Management is using what you have to do what you want to do: using resources (people, money, time, food, equipment, information) to reach the organisation's objectives.

cards.f: Management is often described as getting work done through whom?
cards.b: Through other people. The chef reaches the kitchen's goals with a team, and does it with limited resources, so every resource must be used wisely.

cards.f: Why must a chef allocate resources with care? Give a kitchen example.
cards.b: All six resources are limited. On Saturday the strongest cook goes to the busiest station, not the easiest one: a management decision about a limited resource.

cards.f: List the six resources of a kitchen.
cards.b: People; money; time; food and beverage; equipment and energy; procedures and information. All of them are always limited.

cards.f: Efficiency: define it and give a kitchen example.
cards.b: Doing things right: less waste of food, labour, energy and time. Example: fish trimmings become stock and staff meals instead of going in the bin.

cards.f: Effectiveness: define it and give a kitchen example.
cards.b: Doing the right things: reaching the goals that matter (standard, guest, timing). Example: plates go out to the standard, on time, to satisfied guests.

cards.f: A line sends out cold plates very fast. Efficient, effective, both or neither?
cards.b: Efficient but not effective: quick work, wrong result. The opposite case is effective but not efficient: excellent food, but half the mise en place is thrown away each night.

cards.f: Name the three levels of management with a hotel or kitchen title for each.
cards.b: Top: general manager, food and beverage director. Middle: executive chef, head chef. First-line: sous-chef, chef de partie. Titles depend on the size of the operation.

cards.f: What does a first-line manager do?
cards.b: Supervises, shift by shift, the people who do the work: rotas, prep, portions, service. A chef de partie works alongside the team, so technical skill matters most here.

cards.f: Katz (1955): name the three management skills and who needs them.
cards.b: Technical (how the work is done): mainly first-line. Human (communication, motivation): at every level. Conceptual (the big picture): mainly top managers.

cards.f: Which skill matters most at each level of management?
cards.b: Top: conceptual. Middle: human and conceptual. First-line: technical, because they work with the team. Human skills matter equally at all three levels.

cards.f: Why does the best cook often struggle after promotion to sous-chef?
cards.b: He was promoted for technical skill, but the new job needs human skills: communication, motivation and resolving conflict. Working with and through people is not the same as cooking.

cards.f: List the seven functions of management.
cards.b: Planning, organising, coordinating, staffing, directing, controlling, evaluating (Ninemeier, 2000). In real life they happen at the same time, not in a neat sequence.

cards.f: Match: Drucker, Katz, Fayol, Ninemeier.
cards.b: Drucker (1967): efficiency and effectiveness. Katz (1955): the three management skills. Fayol (1916): management as a set of functions. Ninemeier (2000): the list of seven functions.

cards.f: Planning: what is it, and which four conditions affect it?
cards.b: Setting goals (what we want) and action plans (how we get there). Conditions: information, communication, flexibility, implementation. A plan that is not carried out is only a wish.

cards.f: Organising: which two principles apply?
cards.b: Unity of command: one supervisor for each person. Span of control: how many people one supervisor can manage, depending on experience, complexity of the work and how often problems arise.

cards.f: What does 'we delegate the task, not the responsibility' mean?
cards.b: The chef who delegates a task remains accountable to the general manager. Delegation passes authority down the hierarchy; it does not make the problem someone else's.

cards.f: Staffing: what does it include?
cards.b: Recruitment and selection, job descriptions, interviews and the induction of new staff: finding and keeping the right people (developed in Lecture 5).

cards.f: Directing: name its main elements.
cards.b: Supervision, rotas, discipline, motivation (shared goals) and leading by example. The pre-service briefing is a directing tool: covers, specials, allergies, VIPs, stations.

cards.f: Controlling: what is it?
cards.b: Comparing what actually happens with the standard and correcting the difference, during the work. It applies at every stage where food changes hands.

cards.f: Name the six stages at which food is controlled.
cards.b: Purchasing, receiving, storing (first in, first out), issuing (only with a requisition), production (recipes, yields, portions) and service (every dish charged).

cards.f: Give a controlling example at the receiving stage.
cards.b: The invoice says 20 kg of salmon but 18 arrive. Weigh the delivery and check quantity, quality and temperature against the order, then correct the difference.

cards.f: Controlling or evaluating?
cards.b: Controlling happens during the work, against a standard. Evaluating happens afterwards and looks at overall progress; its lessons go into the next plan.

cards.f: Evaluating: what does it look at?
cards.b: Progress towards the goals, employee performance, training results and corrective action. It closes the cycle: the lessons go into the next round of planning.

cards.f: List the chef's five responsibilities.
cards.b: Food cost and quality; staff and labour cost; equipment and energy; public relations; continuing education. They are also the map of the module.

cards.f: Name the six qualities of a culinary professional beyond technique.
cards.b: Tact and teamwork; integrity; self-control; appearance and hygiene; knowledge and creativity; persistence and patience. Technique is only the entry ticket.

cards.f: The Culinary Institute of America names three core attributes of a professional cook. What are they?
cards.b: Serving the guest, being responsible (for guests, colleagues, food and equipment) and making good judgements. The individual qualities all add up to these three.

cards.f: What do commitment to service and a sense of responsibility cover?
cards.b: Commitment to service: quality and guest satisfaction. Sense of responsibility: towards guests, colleagues, food and equipment.

cards.f: Sound judgement: what is it, and why is it hard to build?
cards.b: Making the right call at the right moment, such as rescuing a split sauce or starting again. It is the slowest to build, so experienced chefs get decisions a talented commis does not.

cards.f: What decides who gets promoted?
cards.b: Technique is the entry ticket. Judgement and self-control earn the promotion; hygiene and appearance give the first impression; honesty builds trust. These qualities are learned, not inborn.

cards.f: Why is reporting a short fish delivery at once a sign of integrity?
cards.b: Hiding a problem always costs more than reporting it early: the kitchen can change the special in time and trust in that cook grows. Colleagues forgive a slow cook more easily than a dishonest one.

cards.f: The path of a professional: name the five steps.
cards.b: Education, apprenticeship, stages, networking, continuing education (seminars, competitions, associations). The path is not always a straight line.

cards.f: What is a stage?
cards.b: A short placement, from a few days to a few months, in another kitchen to see another style and system. Very common in Europe.

cards.f: Name six sources for staying current.
cards.b: Books, trade magazines, professional websites, government publications, training videos and supplier demonstrations. No single source is enough on its own.

cards.f: The chef's three roles: what are they?
cards.b: Executive (mission and plan), administrator (systems: budgets, inventory, schedules) and manager (running the four areas every day). The same chef moves between the three.

cards.f: Name the four areas a chef manages.
cards.b: Physical assets (food, equipment, supplies); information (tastes, trends, costs, regulations); people (jobs, training, rotas); time (operations, training, communication).

cards.f: Assets, information, people, time: one kitchen example of each?
cards.b: Assets: stock control, servicing the combi oven. Information: which dishes sell, allergen rules. People: training the new commis, the rota. Time: a daily prep list.

cards.f: Which two of the four areas do new chefs neglect most?
cards.b: Information and time. Students name physical assets and people first. Time is the scarcest resource, wasted by disorder and by instructions that must be repeated.

cards.f: Name five habits for using time well.
cards.b: Review the day, make time for training, give clear instructions once, keep an orderly workspace, and buy and maintain tools before they fail.

cards.f: Name the six types of foodservice establishment.
cards.b: Hotels and resorts; restaurants; quick service; clubs and corporate dining; institutional catering (hospitals, schools, armed forces); catering, cruise ships and airlines.

cards.f: Why does seasonality matter for chefs in Cyprus?
cards.b: A resort kitchen fully staffed in August may close from December to March, while a hospital runs at the same pace all year. This shapes contracts and careers.

cards.f: Give the career ladder from commis to F&B director.
cards.b: Commis, demi-chef de partie, chef de partie, sous-chef, head chef, executive chef, F&B director. Side paths: pastry, private chef, research, quality, teaching, your own business.

cards.f: Name the six forces that shaped catering.
cards.b: Methods and the trade; farming and food supply; eating out; foods and shelf life; fuel and equipment; nutrition and hygiene. None acted alone.

cards.f: Where and when did the first restaurant in the modern sense open?
cards.b: Paris, 1782: Beauvilliers opened La Grande Taverne de Londres, with a proper menu, separate tables and a wine list.

cards.f: Why is the French Revolution of 1789 linked with the birth of the restaurant?
cards.b: The cooks of aristocratic households lost their employers and opened their own restaurants. The modern restaurant was born from that change.

cards.f: Why did food have to travel after the Industrial Revolution?
cards.b: The population grew fast and moved to towns and cities. Local farms could no longer supply them, so food travelled by road and later by rail, and had to keep longer.

cards.f: Industrial Revolution: what changed in preservation and fuel?
cards.b: Bottling (Appert, 1810), canning and, later, refrigeration developed. Coal replaced wood for cooking, and gas came later.

cards.f: Industrial Revolution: name two changes in eating and drinking habits.
cards.b: Home baking and brewing declined and people bought more of their food. Tea replaced ale as the everyday drink.

cards.f: Carême (1784-1833): what did he contribute?
cards.b: 'King of chefs, chef of kings'; founder of grande cuisine; pièces montées from architectural drawings; sauces organised in families, an early standard like the standard recipe.

cards.f: Soyer (1810-1858): what did he contribute?
cards.b: At the Reform Club, London: cooking with gas and adjustable ovens (1841) and a planned layout of sections. Soup kitchens in the Irish famine (1847); an army field stove in the Crimea.

cards.f: Who created the brigade system, and how does it work?
cards.b: Auguste Escoffier (1846-1935). Work is split into sections; a chef de partie heads each one, and everyone answers up a single chain of command.

cards.f: Escoffier: name his key facts.
cards.b: Apprenticed at 13 in Nice; partner of the hotelier César Ritz (Savoy, Ritz in Paris, Carlton); Le guide culinaire (1903); first chef awarded the Legion of Honour (1920).

cards.f: Why does Escoffier's brigade still matter for management?
cards.b: One station, one chef de partie, one line of authority. He invented a system for organising cooks, designed around the work. Stations, hierarchy, mise en place and the pass survive even in small kitchens.

cards.f: Ranhofer (1836-1899): what did he contribute?
cards.b: Chef de cuisine of Delmonico's, New York, for over three decades; America's first great chef; The Epicurean (1894); Baked Alaska and Lobster Newberg.

cards.f: Which two of the four chefs were contemporaries?
cards.b: Escoffier and Ranhofer. They never worked together, but shaped great kitchens on either side of the Atlantic at the same time.

cards.f: Three milestones after Escoffier.
cards.b: 1900: the Michelin Guide (stars from 1926). 1970s: nouvelle cuisine (lighter, fresher, shorter menus). 2000 onwards: sustainability and data (allergens, local sourcing, social media).

cards.f: The chef's role then and now: compare focus and organisation.
cards.b: Escoffier's time: technique, discipline, hierarchy and a strict brigade. Today: technique plus business, guest and team, in flatter teams cross-trained on several stations.

cards.f: Name the six skills of the modern chef.
cards.b: Communication, maths and costing, planning, quality control, managing people and computer skills.

cards.f: Name three purposes of structure in a professional kitchen.
cards.b: It sets the line of authority and the line of communication; shows who answers and who directs; and shows where responsibility sits and where everyone stands. It is built to the size of the business.

cards.f: How did Escoffier create the partie system?
cards.b: He studied the basic techniques, defined tasks and standards any cook could learn, and grouped them into stations, one chef de partie each, under a chain of command taken from the army.

cards.f: Draw the classical brigade from top to bottom.
cards.b: Chef de cuisine; sous-chef; chefs de partie (saucier, rôtisseur, poissonnier, entremetier, garde manger, pâtissier); commis and apprentices.

cards.f: Saucier, rôtisseur, grillardin, friturier: what does each do?
cards.b: Saucier: sauces, stews, hot starters, sautés. Rôtisseur: roasts, braises, jus. Grillardin: grill. Friturier: fried food. The last two exist as separate stations only in large kitchens.

cards.f: Poissonnier and entremetier: what do they do?
cards.b: Poissonnier: fish, shellfish and their sauces. Entremetier: vegetables, soups and eggs (in large kitchens split into potager for soups and légumier for vegetables).

cards.f: Chef de cuisine or sous-chef: who does what?
cards.b: Chef de cuisine: menu, ordering, costs, staff, standards. Sous-chef: production, schedules, deputising, discipline.

cards.f: What does the garde manger do?
cards.b: The cold section: salads, pâtés, cold first courses and buffet work. Often the biggest section, since it may also take on the butchery. Modern title: pantry cook.

cards.f: Which stations make up the three areas every brigade must cover?
cards.b: Hot kitchen (saucier, rôtisseur, poissonnier, entremetier), cold kitchen (garde manger) and pastry (pâtissier). Large, medium and small brigades all cover the same three areas, with fewer named people.

cards.f: What is a tournant?
cards.b: The swing cook who steps in wherever a section is short, for example on days off. Not a section of its own: one of three extra roles around the brigade.

cards.f: Name the three roles around the brigade that are not stations.
cards.b: Tournant: covers any station. Communard: cooks the staff meals. Aboyeur: calls the orders at the pass (modern title: expediter).

cards.f: Pâtissier and the support posts: who does what?
cards.b: Pâtissier: desserts, bread, ice cream. Boucher: butchery. Plongeur or marmiton: dishes and pots. Commis: junior cook under a chef de partie. Apprentice: still formally learning.

cards.f: Why do today's brigades combine stations? Name four reasons.
cards.b: Equipment (combi, sous vide); simpler, lighter menus; expensive labour; and ready-prepared, portioned products. Combining stations is a sensible answer to cost, not a lower standard.

cards.f: What does a small brigade look like?
cards.b: A chef de cuisine who cooks; a sous-chef working as saucier and poissonnier; garde manger and pâtissier with an assistant; a plongeur and a vegetable assistant.

cards.f: What stays the same in a brigade of any size?
cards.b: Fewer titles, but always someone for cold, hot and sweet. The principle is combining stations, with one person in charge of each and one supervisor for each person.

cards.f: Name the five principles of kitchen design.
cards.b: Functionality, self-sufficiency, health and safety, flexibility, aesthetics. The key idea: flow in one direction from receiving to service.

cards.f: Name the four kitchen layouts.
cards.b: Island (ranges in the centre, easy supervision); zones (sections along the walls); production line (short menu, little movement); open kitchen (visible to guests, built on another layout).

cards.f: Why is lighting a working tool?
cards.b: Safety (slips, burns, cuts), quality (doneness, colour, presentation), speed under pressure and food safety (spotting dirt and pests).

cards.f: Give the modern equivalents of chef de cuisine, sous-chef and chef de partie.
cards.b: Kitchen manager or food service director = chef de cuisine. Assistant manager = sous-chef. Lead cook or head cook = chef de partie. Second and third cook = demi-chef de partie and commis.

cards.f: Other modern titles: pantry cook, butcher, pastry chef, expediter.
cards.b: Pantry cook = garde manger. Butcher = boucher. Pastry chef or baker = pâtissier. Expediter = aboyeur. The change is in the language, not in what the job demands.

cards.f: Why does a resort kitchen have layers of sous-chefs?
cards.b: The kitchen runs several parallel businesses (à la carte, banqueting, buffet, pastry), each with its own sous-chef under an executive sous-chef. The stations did not change.

cards.f: What does it mean that the chef works 'in the middle'?
cards.b: Management sees the chef as staff, and the staff see the chef as management. The chef translates instructions from above into instructions the team can use.

cards.f: List the chef's five management responsibilities.
cards.b: Planning; organising and coordinating; motivating (money and recognition); controlling; accountability and discipline.

cards.f: Control or discipline: what is the difference?
cards.b: Control is about the system: understood by everyone, catches problems early, includes correction. Discipline is about the person: respect and a positive approach, not only punishment.

cards.f: What is the informal hierarchy?
cards.b: Often the most experienced commis or the longest-serving member: not on the chart, but their opinion counts. A wise chef works with that person, not against them.

cards.f: Job description or job specification: what is the difference?
cards.b: Job description: the job (title, reporting line, purpose, main duties). Job specification: the person (qualifications, skills, experience, personal qualities).

cards.f: Which rows of a job profile form the job specification?
cards.b: For a chef de partie (saucier), the requirements row: culinary qualification, hot-station experience, sauces, speed. Title, reports to, supervises, purpose and main duties form the job description.

cards.f: Job specification: is it about the job or the person, and what does it list?
cards.b: The person: qualifications, skills, experience and personal qualities. Remember: the description is about the job; the specification is about the person.

cards.f: Name the eight steps of recruitment.
cards.b: Need; description and specification; advertising; applications and shortlist; interview; practical test; references; offer and contract.

cards.f: Induction: what happens on day one, and why does it matter?
cards.b: Meet the team, tour the whole kitchen, uniform, hygiene and safety rules. Resignations often start in the first weeks, and exit interviews show why people really leave.

cards.f: How do training and appraisal work together?
cards.b: Appraisal finds the gap, training closes it, and the next appraisal checks. Training targets a real gap and measures results; appraisal is regular, with feedback people can act on.

cards.f: Progressive discipline: name the four steps.
cards.b: Verbal warning (in private, straight away); written warning (signed by both); final warning (a clear deadline); dismissal (only with policy and law). Documented, fair, the same for everyone.

cards.f: What is the aim of discipline in a kitchen?
cards.b: To correct, not to punish. It is documented, fair and consistent, follows company policy and employment law, and the chef wants the employee to succeed, not to leave.

cards.f: Explain McGregor's hot stove rule.
cards.b: Discipline should be immediate, with warning, consistent and impersonal: like touching a hot stove, it burns at once, everyone knows beforehand, it burns anyone, and the act is judged, not the person.

cards.f: Give the two definitions of leadership.
cards.b: Leadership by position and authority, or by inspiration, whatever the title. The best leaders combine both. Authority without respect brings only obedience.

cards.f: Are leaders born or made?
cards.b: Made. The old 'you have it or you don't' view is inadequate. Leadership is built through training, feedback and practice, so it can be taught.

cards.f: Name the six qualities of a kitchen leader.
cards.b: Reliable and fair; calm and decisive; good judgement; initiative; strong with people; respected (philotimo).

cards.f: What is philotimo?
cards.b: A sense of duty and honour that makes a leader keep a promise even when nobody checks. It does not translate easily.

cards.f: What are Baskette's three kinds of leadership?
cards.b: By authority (the position), by inspiration (example, fairness, constancy of purpose) and impartial (recognising every contribution). A chef needs all three at once.

cards.f: Leadership by authority: strength and risk?
cards.b: Based on the position, it gives a clear hierarchy from day one. Risk: respect is not automatic, and the power can be abused. Authority without respect brings only obedience.

cards.f: Leadership by inspiration: how is it earned?
cards.b: Through behaviour, not position: example, fairness, constancy of purpose, hard work and listening. It works at every level, even a commis, and is earned continuously, so it can be lost.

cards.f: What is impartial leadership?
cards.b: Recognising every contribution and everyone's strengths and weaknesses; counselling rather than criticising, correcting rather than punishing. Example: showing the right pan temperature instead of shouting.

cards.f: Autocratic style: how it works, when it suits, what is the risk?
cards.b: The leader decides, without explanation. It suits new staff and emergencies, such as a fryer fire. Overused, it brings low morale, absence and resignations.

cards.f: Name the three classic styles and the study they come from.
cards.b: Autocratic (leader decides), democratic (staff take part), laissez-faire (the employee decides). Lewin, Lippitt and White, 1939. None is always right: the test is the person and the moment.

cards.f: Democratic and laissez-faire: when do they suit?
cards.b: Democratic: an experienced team with a shared problem; decisions are slower. Laissez-faire: motivated specialists only; it looks like no leadership and has the most limited use in a kitchen.

cards.f: How do you recognise the autocratic style in a case?
cards.b: Orders without explanation; the leader keeps the difficult tasks and decisions; changes made without consulting or informing anyone; reliance on position rather than inspiration.

cards.f: The cook who is late three days running: how does each style respond?
cards.b: Autocratic: 'Eight o'clock sharp, or we have a problem' (compliance, resentment). Democratic: 'Let's find a solution together' (finds the real cause). Laissez-faire: 'You'll sort it out' (manages nothing).

cards.f: Situational leadership: which two questions decide the style?
cards.b: How competent is this person at this task, and how much confidence and commitment do they have now? The style follows the person (Hersey and Blanchard).

cards.f: Name the four situational styles and who needs each.
cards.b: Telling: a new commis, clear steps and close supervision. Selling: losing confidence. Participating: able but unsure. Delegating: an experienced chef de partie, who gets the station and its decisions.

cards.f: Selling or participating: what is the difference?
cards.b: Selling: a developing cook losing confidence needs the reasoning and encouragement. Participating: an able cook who is unsure already knows the technique and needs support, not more instructions.

cards.f: Constancy of purpose: what does it mean?
cards.b: A leader's standards do not change with mood or pressure: the same chef on a quiet Tuesday and a crazy Saturday. The reward is trust.

cards.f: Name the six habits that build constancy of purpose during one shift.
cards.b: Plan, greet everyone, set priorities with the key people, prevent instead of firefighting, be available during service, and review your own performance.

cards.f: Leading by example: name the six behaviours.
cards.b: Ready and present; plans ahead; technically current; meets the standard every time; shares information and skills; honest and grateful. None of them needs a title.

cards.f: How does a good leader build leaders?
cards.b: Delegates responsibility, not only tasks; lets experienced staff run training and briefings; surrounds themselves with committed, capable people; prepares successors.

cards.f: Case: what did Earl get wrong?
cards.b: He relied on authority, kept his distance, accepted no feedback, spoke to the team only at the daily briefing and stopped developing himself. He lacked leadership by inspiration and constancy of purpose.

mcq.q: A head chef asks you what 'managing' a kitchen really means. Which answer fits the definition from Lecture 1?
o: Reducing the whole kitchen's spending to the bare minimum each month
Personally taking charge of every critical job in the kitchen
Getting the team to meet the goals without wasting scarce resources
Perfecting the quality of every single dish that leaves the pass
mcq.e: Management is achieving objectives through people with limited resources: using what you have to do what you want to do. The traps are doing everything yourself, cooking well, or only cutting cost.

mcq.q: On Saturday the head chef puts the strongest cook on the busiest station instead of the easiest one. Which idea from Lecture 1 does this show?
o: Checking the portions of every dish at the receiving stage
Putting a limited resource, people, where it adds the most value
Giving each person only one supervisor to answer to
Delegating the task while keeping the responsibility for it
mcq.e: The chef decides where each of the six limited resources goes. Here the resource is people (skills and hours), and the decision is about allocation, not about unity of command.

mcq.q: A banqueting team clears every ticket in record time, but a third of the dishes reach the guests lukewarm. How would you describe this team?
o: Strong on both counts, because every ticket was cleared quickly
Effective in its result, yet inefficient in its use of time
Weak on both counts, because speed is not a measure of either quality
Efficient with its time, yet ineffective because the result is wrong
mcq.e: Efficiency is doing things right, with little waste of time or food. Effectiveness is doing the right things, here dishes at the standard the guest expects. Fast work with a poor result is efficient but not effective.

mcq.q: In a resort kitchen, who supervises the cooks doing the actual work, shift by shift, and so counts as a first-line manager?
o: A chef de partie who supervises the commis working on one station
The person who sets the long-term direction of the whole hotel
The executive chef who coordinates the departments of a large resort
The director responsible for all the food and beverage outlets
mcq.e: First-line managers supervise the people who do the work, like sous-chefs and chefs de partie. Top managers (general manager, F&B director) set direction; middle managers (executive or head chef) turn plans into operating plans.

mcq.q: A chef de partie spends most of the shift working next to the commis. According to Katz, which skill is the most important at this level?
o: Human skill alone, because technique no longer matters after a promotion
All three skills in equal measure, whatever the level of management
Technical skill, because they work beside the team and show how the work is done
Conceptual skill, because they must see how the kitchen fits the market and the future
mcq.e: First-line managers need technical skill most; conceptual skill is mainly for top managers; human skills matter at every level. The mix changes with the level, so the three skills are not equal everywhere.

mcq.q: A commis takes instructions from both the sous-chef and the pastry chef, and the two sometimes clash. Which principle of organising is being broken?
o: Span of control: a supervisor should manage only a few people
Flexibility: a plan should adjust to changing circumstances
Delegation: authority should be passed down to each level
Unity of command: each person should have one supervisor
mcq.e: Unity of command means one supervisor for each person; with two bosses, clashing orders are only a matter of time. Span of control is about how many people one supervisor can manage.

mcq.q: A new prep sheet has been written and everyone knows about it, but it stays in the office and is never used. Which condition of good planning has failed?
o: Implementation: a plan that is not carried out is only a wish
Communication, because the plan was never explained properly
Information, because the plan was based on incomplete facts
Flexibility, because the plan could not adjust when things changed
mcq.e: The four conditions are information, communication, flexibility and implementation. Here the plan exists and is known, but it is not put into practice, so implementation has failed.

mcq.q: A head chef delegates the weekly food order to a chef de partie, and the order turns out wrong. Who is still accountable to the general manager?
o: The chef de partie, because the task is now entirely theirs
The head chef, because we delegate the task and not the responsibility
The supplier, because the delivery came from outside the kitchen
Nobody, because delegation moved the responsibility down the hierarchy
mcq.e: Delegation passes the task and the authority down, but the chef who delegates stays accountable. Thinking 'it is not my problem any more' is the common mistake.

mcq.q: On a wedding day the chef agrees the serving times with the banqueting and service teams so that every department works together. Which function is this?
o: Staffing: finding two extra cooks for the day
Organising: giving each station its tasks
Planning: setting the menu and quantities with the client
Coordinating: bringing the departments together
mcq.e: Coordinating is departments working together, here through agreed timings. Organising is who does what, planning is menu, quantities and orders, and staffing is, for example, the two extra cooks.

mcq.q: On Friday the head chef weighs portions at the pass, compares each one with the recipe card and has the cook correct any difference. Which function of management is this?
o: Directing: supervising and motivating people day to day
Controlling: checking results against a standard and correcting them
Coordinating: bringing departments together at the right moment
Evaluating: reviewing overall progress after the work is done
mcq.e: Controlling compares what actually happens with the standard during the work and corrects the difference. Evaluating looks back at overall progress afterwards, which is the usual trap.

mcq.q: Which control belongs to the issuing stage of the food cycle?
o: Releasing stock from the store only against a requisition
Making sure that every dish that is served is also charged
Weighing each delivery against the invoice before signing for it
Rotating the stock on a strict first-in, first-out basis
mcq.e: Issuing is the point where food leaves the store, and it should happen only with a requisition. Weighing deliveries is receiving, first in first out is storing, and charging every dish is service.

mcq.q: A sauce splits ten minutes before service and the chef de partie knows at once whether to rescue it or start again. Which of the three core attributes named by the Culinary Institute of America does this show?
o: Creativity: dishes with taste as well as technique
A sense of responsibility towards guests, colleagues, food and equipment
Sound judgement: the right call at the right moment
Commitment to service: putting guest satisfaction first
mcq.e: The three core attributes are commitment to service, a sense of responsibility and sound judgement. Deciding correctly under pressure is judgement; creativity is one of the six qualities but not one of the three core attributes.

mcq.q: Which set describes the four areas a chef must manage, according to Lecture 2?
o: Planning, organising, directing and controlling
Food cost, labour cost, equipment and public relations
Physical assets, information, people and time
Executive, administrator, manager and technician
mcq.e: The four areas are physical assets (food, equipment, supplies), information, people and time. The other sets are the chef's responsibilities, management functions and roles.

mcq.q: A chef designs the budgets, the inventory control and the allergen records that make the kitchen's goals real. Which of the chef's roles is this?
o: The administrator role
The manager role
The technician role
The executive role
mcq.e: The administrator builds the systems that make the plan real: budgets, inventory control, schedules, allergen records. The executive sets the mission and plan; the manager runs the four areas day to day.

mcq.q: A cook finds at receiving that part of the fish order is missing. What does a culinary professional do?
o: Waits to see whether service actually runs out of the dish
Tells the sous-chef at once so the special can be changed
Substitutes another fish quietly and hopes nobody notices
Mentions it after service, once the pressure is all over
mcq.e: Hiding a problem always costs more than reporting it early. Honesty builds trust, and a kitchen forgives a slow cook more easily than a dishonest one.

mcq.q: In a chef's career, what is a 'stage'?
o: The final practical exam taken at the end of culinary school
A fixed rank between commis and chef de partie in the brigade
A national competition held every year for young chefs
A short placement in another kitchen to see a different system
mcq.e: A stage lasts from a few days to a few months and is common in Europe. It is a step on the path of a professional, together with education, apprenticeship, networking and continuing education.

mcq.q: Which habit makes the best use of time, the scarcest resource, according to Lecture 2?
o: Repeating each instruction several times to be quite sure
Skipping training in busy periods in order to save hours
Spending fifteen minutes each morning on yesterday's orders
Repairing tools only after they have failed during service
mcq.e: The five habits are reviewing the day, making time for training, giving clear instructions once, keeping an orderly workspace and maintaining tools before they fail.

mcq.q: Which type of foodservice establishment is defined mainly by speed and standardisation?
o: Restaurants
Hotels and resorts
Clubs and corporate dining
Quick service
mcq.e: Quick service is defined by speed and standardisation. Restaurants by quality and consistency, clubs by a small regular clientele, hotels and resorts by volume and seasonality.

mcq.q: In the traditional career ladder inside the brigade, which post comes directly after chef de partie?
o: Head chef, who leads the team
Sous-chef, who runs the service
Executive chef, who runs a large operation
Demi-chef de partie, who assists the chef de partie
mcq.e: The ladder runs commis, demi-chef de partie, chef de partie, sous-chef, head chef, executive chef and F&B director. The demi-chef de partie comes before the chef de partie, not after it.

mcq.q: Which statement correctly describes a change brought by the Industrial Revolution?
o: Towns grew too fast for local farms to feed them, so food began to travel
Home baking and brewing increased as people moved into the cities
Tea gave way to ale as the everyday drink of the growing towns
Wood replaced coal as the main cooking fuel in the new city kitchens
mcq.e: Population growth and the move to cities meant food had to travel. The other options reverse real changes: coal replaced wood, home baking and brewing declined, and tea replaced ale.

mcq.q: Why is the French Revolution of 1789 linked with the birth of the restaurant?
o: Cooks of aristocratic households lost their employers and opened restaurants
Beauvilliers closed his tavern and moved his cooks across to London
Food shortages forced hotels and inns to ration the meals they could serve
The new republic ordered every inn and tavern to publish a printed menu
mcq.e: After 1789 the cooks of the aristocracy had no employers, so they opened restaurants. The modern restaurant was born from that change.

mcq.q: Carême organised the French sauces into families. Which modern management idea is this an early example of?
o: Unity of command: every person in the kitchen has one supervisor only
Delegating a task while keeping the responsibility for the result
A span of control matched to a supervisor's experience and workload
A standard system any trained cook can follow for a consistent result
mcq.e: Sauce families gave cooks a system to follow for a consistent result, which is the idea behind the standard recipe today.

mcq.q: Which chef is credited with creating the brigade, the station-based team structure that most professional kitchens still follow?
o: Alexis Soyer, who ran the Reform Club kitchen in London
Auguste Escoffier, the partner of the hotelier César Ritz
Marie-Antoine Carême, who organised the sauces into families
Charles Ranhofer, the chef of Delmonico's in New York
mcq.e: Escoffier divided the kitchen into stations, each led by a chef de partie, with one line of authority. Carême is known for sauce families, Soyer for gas and a planned layout, Ranhofer for Delmonico's.

mcq.q: Soyer's 1841 kitchen at the Reform Club had a planned layout of sections. Which later system did this anticipate?
o: The sauce families
The Michelin star system
The brigade of stations
Nouvelle cuisine
mcq.e: A kitchen planned in sections, each with its own work, anticipates the brigade that Escoffier later developed. Soyer also cooked with gas and ran soup kitchens during the Irish famine.

mcq.q: Which movement of the 1970s reacted against heavy classical cooking with lighter sauces, fresh ingredients and shorter menus?
o: Sustainable sourcing
The brigade system
Nouvelle cuisine
Grande cuisine
mcq.e: Nouvelle cuisine reacted against the heavy classical style that Escoffier had simplified but not abandoned. Sustainability and data belong to the 21st century.

mcq.q: Which skill of the modern chef would have meant nothing to Escoffier's brigade?
o: Planning (orders, rotas and forecasting)
Computer skills (ordering and costing)
Quality control (consistent standards)
Communication (team, guests, suppliers)
mcq.e: Computer skills is the only one of the six that did not exist in some form in Escoffier's time. Planning, quality control, communication, costing and managing people existed in his brigade on a smaller scale.

mcq.q: Which chef ran the kitchen of Delmonico's in New York and wrote The Epicurean (1894)?
o: Charles Ranhofer
Alexis Soyer
Marie-Antoine Carême
Auguste Escoffier
mcq.e: Ranhofer, born in France, was America's first great chef at Delmonico's. Baked Alaska and Lobster Newberg are linked with him.

mcq.q: The cold buffet, the pâtés and the salads for a banquet are prepared by which part of the classical brigade?
o: The saucier of the classical brigade
The entremetier of the classical brigade
The tournant of the classical brigade
The garde manger of the classical brigade
mcq.e: The garde manger runs the cold kitchen. The saucier handles sauces and sautés, the entremetier vegetables, soups and eggs, and the tournant is a relief cook, not a station.

mcq.q: On Saturday the saucier is ill, and the chef needs a cook who can step into any station. Which post exists for this purpose?
o: The tournant of the classical brigade
The aboyeur of the classical brigade
The communard of the classical brigade
The commis of the classical brigade
mcq.e: The tournant is the relief cook who covers any station. The communard cooks the staff meals, the aboyeur calls the orders at the pass, and the commis is a junior cook under one chef de partie.

mcq.q: With only 60 seats, a bistro cannot afford the full classical brigade. Which smaller team still covers the hot, cold and sweet work at the lowest labour cost?
o: A hot kitchen only, with the cold dishes and the desserts left off the menu in order to save on staff
A chef de cuisine and four commis, with nobody in charge of the cold work, the hot work or the pastry
A full classical brigade, with a separate chef de partie for every station but only one commis for the whole kitchen
A chef de cuisine who cooks, a sous-chef for sauces and fish, a garde manger and pâtissier with an assistant, and a plongeur
mcq.e: Small brigades combine stations, such as a sous-chef working as saucier and poissonnier, but there is still someone for cold, hot and sweet. Lower labour cost, a shorter menu, modern equipment and prepared products make this possible.

mcq.q: Which chef de partie is responsible for roasts, braises and jus?
o: The grillardin
The poissonnier
The rôtisseur
The entremetier
mcq.e: The rôtisseur handles roasts, braises and jus. The grillardin (grill) is separate only in large kitchens; otherwise the rôtisseur covers it.

mcq.q: Which post deputises for the chef de cuisine and looks after production and schedules?
o: The aboyeur
The sous-chef
The saucier
The tournant
mcq.e: The sous-chef handles production, schedules, deputising and discipline. The chef de cuisine is above, responsible for menu, ordering, costs, staff and standards.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a commis and an apprentice?
o: The commis is trained and paid as staff; the apprentice is still formally learning
There is no difference between them, as the two titles mean the same thing
The apprentice is trained and paid as staff, while the commis is still formally learning
The commis runs a station, while the apprentice only washes dishes and pots
mcq.e: A commis is a junior cook who works under a chef de partie and is paid as staff. An apprentice learns under supervision. Dishes and pots belong to the plongeur or marmiton.

mcq.q: Which principle of kitchen design means that each section can work on its own, without cooks leaving it all the time?
o: Functionality
Aesthetics
Self-sufficiency
Flexibility
mcq.e: Self-sufficiency is about each section working on its own. Functionality is the smooth overall flow between sections, in one direction from receiving to service. People often confuse the two.

mcq.q: A souvlaki shop with a very short menu, where staff hardly need to move, is most likely to use which kitchen layout?
o: Open kitchen
Production line
Zones
Island
mcq.e: A production line suits a short menu and little movement. Island and zones suit large kitchens such as banqueting; an open kitchen is a presentation choice built on another layout.

mcq.q: Which development helps to explain why today's brigades are simpler than the classical one?
o: Labour has become cheaper than the equipment in the kitchen
Fresh, unprepared products need much more work in the kitchen
Menus have become longer and more complex over the years
Combi ovens and sous vide now do work that needed extra staff
mcq.e: Equipment, simpler and lighter menus, expensive labour and ready-prepared products all reduce the need for separate stations. The other options say the opposite.

mcq.q: Which line in a job advert for a garde manger belongs to the job specification and not to the job description?
o: Supervises the commis and apprentices on the station
Prepares the salads, pâtés and cold buffet every day
A culinary qualification and cold-kitchen experience
Reports to the sous-chef on the evening shift
mcq.e: The job description describes the job (title, reporting line, duties); the job specification describes the person who could do it: qualifications, skills and experience.

mcq.q: Which order of steps is used in progressive discipline in a kitchen?
o: Verbal warning, written warning, final warning, dismissal
Written warning, verbal warning, final warning, dismissal
Verbal warning, final warning, written warning, dismissal
Final warning, verbal warning, written warning, dismissal
mcq.e: Discipline progresses step by step, and each step is documented, fair and consistent with policy and law. The aim is to correct behaviour, not to punish, so a first mistake should not jump straight to a final warning or dismissal.

mcq.q: In a modern hotel advert, the 'assistant manager' of the kitchen corresponds to which classical post?
o: Chef de cuisine
Sous-chef
Demi-chef de partie
Chef de partie
mcq.e: Modern titles borrow from general management. The kitchen manager is the chef de cuisine, the assistant manager the sous-chef and the lead cook the chef de partie.

mcq.q: Head office sets a food cost target, and the chef turns it into a portion rule that the commis follows at the pass. Which idea does this show?
o: The informal hierarchy of the longest-serving member of the team
Unity of command: every person in the kitchen has one supervisor only
Delegating the task and the responsibility to the commis at the pass
The chef works in the middle, translating orders from above for the team
mcq.e: Management sees the chef as staff and the team sees the chef as management, so the chef acts as a translator between the two.

mcq.q: A long-serving commis is not on the organisation chart, yet everyone follows her opinion. What is the wise approach for the chef?
o: Work with her, because every kitchen has an informal hierarchy
Move her to another section so that her influence disappears
Give her formal authority over every station straight away
Ignore her, because only the organisation chart decides who leads
mcq.e: The informal hierarchy is often the most experienced commis or the longest-serving member. A wise chef works with that person and does not fight them.

mcq.q: In the eight steps of recruitment, which step comes straight after the interview?
o: The offer and the signed contract of employment
Advertising the post in schools and on job sites
The practical test, when the candidate cooks for you
Checking references with previous employers
mcq.e: The steps run: need, description and specification, advertising, applications, interview, practical test, references, offer and contract. References come after the practical test.

mcq.q: A chef gives every cook who breaks the same rule exactly the same response. Which quality of McGregor's hot stove rule is this?
o: Impersonal
Consistent
With warning
Immediate
mcq.e: The stove burns anyone who touches it: the same response for everyone. Impersonal is different: the act is judged, not the person.

mcq.q: Which training is most likely to pay off, according to Lecture 5?
o: A course chosen only because a supplier offers it for free
A general yearly course where only attendance is recorded
A course for the whole team, so that everyone gets a certificate
A course aimed at a real gap, with the results checked afterwards
mcq.e: Appraisal finds the gap and training closes it. Training that pays off is tied to the station's standard and measures results, not attendance.

mcq.q: Which of Lewin, Lippitt and White's styles leaves the supervisor holding on to the decisions, while the team is told what to do?
o: The democratic style of leadership
The laissez-faire style of leadership
Impartial leadership, as Baskette describes it
The autocratic style of leadership
mcq.e: In the autocratic style the leader decides, without explanation. Democratic leaders involve staff, laissez-faire leaders leave the decision to the employee, and impartial leadership is about recognising every contribution.

mcq.q: Eleni has just been promoted to sous-chef in a 120-room hotel in Limassol. She announces a new prep routine without saying why, does the sauces herself because it is quicker, and changes two cooks' days off by text message the night before. Which style is she using?
o: Autocratic: she decides alone and gives orders without explaining them
Impartial: she recognises every contribution but corrects firmly
Democratic: she shares decisions but takes over the hard tasks herself
Laissez-faire: she leaves the cooks to decide their own days off
mcq.e: Orders without explanation, keeping the difficult tasks and changing the rota without consulting anyone are signs of the autocratic style. Nothing in the case shows the team taking part in decisions.

mcq.q: Andreas supervises two people at a hotel in Nicosia: a commis in her first week and a chef de partie with ten years' experience who runs the grill. Which pair of approaches fits situational leadership?
o: Telling both of them exactly what to do, so the standard is the same everywhere
Delegating the station to the commis so she learns fast; telling the chef de partie what to do
Telling for the commis, with clear steps; delegating the station to the chef de partie
Delegating to both of them, so that nobody feels controlled or watched
mcq.e: Situational leadership matches the style to the person's competence and confidence: a new commis needs telling, an experienced chef de partie is ready for delegating. Using one style for everyone ignores the person.

mcq.q: Katerina is the new sous-chef in a 90-room hotel in Larnaca. Her cooks often start prep without knowing the day's covers, specials or allergy alerts. Which action should she take first, and which function does it apply?
o: Check every delivery against the invoice herself: controlling
Hold a short briefing before each shift: directing and coordinating
Redraw the organisation chart at the start of each year: organising
Hire two extra cooks for the whole summer season: staffing
mcq.e: A short pre-shift briefing on covers, specials and allergy alerts is a directing and coordinating tool. The other actions use real functions but do not solve the problem that the cooks do not know what is expected.

mcq.q: A commis of two months is always the first to help a struggling colleague, and the section turns to her on a hard night. What kind of leadership does she show?
o: Leadership by authority, because the whole section follows her
Impartial leadership, because she recognises everyone's work equally
No leadership at all, because she has no management title
Leadership by inspiration, which rests on behaviour, not on a title
mcq.e: Leadership by inspiration is earned by example, even at the lowest level. Authority comes from the position, which a commis of two months does not have.

mcq.q: A commis burns a batch of halloumi for a banquet. Which response shows impartial leadership?
o: The chef de partie shouts at the commis in front of the whole section
The chef de partie moves the commis to dish duty as a punishment
The chef de partie shows the right pan temperature and timing on the spot
The chef de partie says nothing, because the banquet is over
mcq.e: Impartial leaders counsel rather than criticise and correct rather than punish. The mistake is put right and the commis is not humiliated.

mcq.q: Which situation suits the democratic style best?
o: An experienced team solving a shared problem together
A motivated specialist who needs no direction at all
A new commis working a first shift in the kitchen
A fryer fire breaking out in the middle of service
mcq.e: The democratic style suits an experienced team with a shared problem, at the cost of slower decisions. New staff and emergencies suit the autocratic style; motivated specialists suit laissez-faire.

mcq.q: An able cook who knows the technique is unsure of himself after a bad service. Which approach fits situational leadership?
o: Telling: step-by-step instructions and close supervision
Participating: give support, not more instructions
Delegating: hand over the station and its decisions without support
Laissez-faire: leave him alone to recover
mcq.e: An able but unsure cook already knows the technique, so support helps more than extra instructions. Telling suits a new commis, and delegating suits an experienced, confident chef de partie.

mcq.q: Which behaviour best shows constancy of purpose?
o: Applying the rules strictly only when the general manager is watching
Changing the priorities of the day with the mood of the team
Keeping the same standard on a quiet Tuesday and on a crazy Saturday
Tightening the standards whenever the chef is stressed
mcq.e: Constancy of purpose means a leader's standards do not change with mood or pressure. The reward is trust.

mcq.q: Earl has 25 years' experience but no training in the last five. He speaks to his team only at the daily briefing and accepts no suggestions, and half the team call in sick. What is the underlying leadership problem?
o: The staff are too young to accept any kind of leader at all
He relies almost only on authority and has stopped developing
He is too democratic: the staff decide everything and he follows
He lacks technical skill and cannot cook to the required standard
mcq.e: Earl keeps his distance, relies on his position and has stopped developing, so there is no leadership by inspiration. His technical skills are excellent, and the staff's youth is his excuse, not the cause.
